rapidFireQAs.q: A 28-year-old man comes to the physician in August for a 1-week history of unsteady gait and visual disturbance. He is an avid traveler and spent most of the year driving between countries in Europe. Physical examination shows difficulty standing with his eyes closed. Ophthalmologic examination shows pupils that change size with moving objects near the eye but do not change size in response to light. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these ophthalmologic findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: A) Argyll-Robertson pupils. (Argyll-Robertson pupils). Diagnosis is neurosyphilis. Argyll-Robertson pupils are colloquially known as “prostitute’s pupils” because they accommodate (to object distance) but don’t react (to light). The patient has a positive Romberg sign, which indicates the etiology for his ataxia is the dorsal columns. This is due to tabes dorsalis as part of the neurosyphilis. But the tabes dorsalis itself is not the cause of the eye findings. The question asks for the most likely explanation for these ophthalmologic findings. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia and medial longitudinal fasciculus syndrome are the same thing, which is how you know they’re both wrong. This is seen in multiple sclerosis on USMLE. I talked about INO/MLF syndrome in detail earlier in this PDF. Weber syndrome is a midbrain stroke that causes ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral spastic paresis of the body. It shows up on the NBME exam for Step 1. But “showing up” doesn’t = HY. There’s like one question on it out of thousands

rapidFireQAs.q: A 28-year-old man from Indonesia undergoes a physical prior to enrollment in the military. He is a routine heavy partier and uses various drugs. He cannot read the number within the yellow circle below. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: B) Ethambutol. (ethambutol). Ethambutol is a drug used to treat tuberculosis that can cause red-green color-blindness. Digoxin can cause yellow, wavy “Vincent van Gogh vision.” Heroin and opioids cause pinpoint pupils. Organophosphates (unrelated) are also a HY cause of pinpoint pupils on USMLE. LSD can cause visual hallucinations. PCP causes vertical and horizontal nystagmus. Rifampin is a drug used to treat tuberculosis that causes red-orange tears and sweat. Sildenafil (Viagra) can cause blue haze. Pilots must avoid taking this prior to flying

rapidFireQAs.q: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a rash on her hands. Which of the following additional findings is most likely to be seen in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) Violaceous eyelids. (violaceous eyelids). The image is a spot-diagnosis for Gottron papules in dermatomyositis. Patients can also get heliotrope rash, which refers to violaceous eyelids or a periorbital rash. Do not confuse this with the malar rash in SLE. Abnormal blinking could be seen in absence seizure, Tourette syndrome, or as a provisional tic disorder in pediatrics. Orbital xanthomata (xanthelasma) are lipid deposits seen periorbitally in patients either idiopathically or secondary to dyslipidemia. Limbal rings refer to the distribution of greater density of pigmentation circumferentially within the iris. These are a normal finding and are more pronounced in the youth. Corneal arcus is lipid deposition seen circumferentially within the iris in patients either idiopathically due to age or secondary to dyslipidemia. HY OPHTHAL

rapidFireQAs.q: There are other details regarding stroke I will discuss in this PDF, but for starters, these risk factors are pass-level points for understanding how/why most strokes occur – i.e., “How do most strokes occur?”
rapidFireQAs.a: “Oh, well the patient will usually have carotid stenosis from HTN, where an atheromatous plaque has launched off, or will have AF, where an LA mural thrombus has launched off.” Simple.

rapidFireQAs.q: In other words, you’ll get a vignette of Wegener, and then you’re like, “Wait, why does he/she have wrist drop though?
rapidFireQAs.a: ” That’s just mononeuritis multiplex.

rapidFireQAs.q: Causes Marcus Gunn pupil (aka relative afferent pupillary defect). In this case, the intensity of light is under-sensed by the affected eye (afferent signal), so the resultant efferent CN III (oculomotor) parasympathetic output (back to the eyes for pupillary constriction) is attenuated; this means when you shine a light in the affected eye, both pupils constrict less in comparison to when the light is shone in the unaffected eye; this gives the mere impression that the pupils dilate when light is shone in the affected eye. Still confusing?
rapidFireQAs.a: Take a look at the following illustration (assuming a lesion of the patient’s right eye [left side of illustration]): MLF syndrome

rapidFireQAs.q: Can be caused by autoimmune diseases. For example, if they give you a 1-liner where they say, “44-year- old woman with SLE has ring-enhancing lesion on CT”
rapidFireQAs.a: CNS lymphoma, not Toxo.

rapidFireQAs.q: ↑ ICP causes compression of intracerebral vessels
rapidFireQAs.a: chemoreceptors sense ↓ oxygen delivery + ↑ CO2 → this causes sympathetic activation and vasoconstriction of peripheral arterioles → ↑ BP → ↑ stretch of carotid sinus baroreceptors → ↑ CN IX afferent firing to solitary nucleus of medulla → ↑ CN X efferent firing to nodal tissue → ↓ HR.

rapidFireQAs.q: NBME will give you a big 15-line paragraph with patient who’s been in an accident + has hypertension + ask you for the reason for his or her HTN
rapidFireQAs.a: “increased intracranial pressure.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Don’t confuse Cushing reflex with Cushing ulcer (completely unrelated), which is head trauma causing vagal outflow
rapidFireQAs.a: increased acid production + peptic ulcers. Glasgow coma scale (GCS)

rapidFireQAs.q: A = CN III (oculomotor) lesion
rapidFireQAs.a: presents as down and out. Can be idiopathic or in Weber syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: C = CN VI (abducens) lesion
rapidFireQAs.a: medially directed eye. Commonly seen with cavernous sinus thrombosis. Cranial nerve exit points

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + 1-wk Hx of R-sided weakness + L-sided inability to feel temperature/pain + diminished vibratory sensation over R foot + brisk R-sided reflexes + R-sided Babinski sign; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on NBME is Brown-Sequard syndrome secondary to viral infection.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient with restless leg syndrome is at increased risk for what disease later in life?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on USMLE = Parkinson disease (if D2 agonist can Tx, then lack of dopamine transmission may be etiology in some patients).

rapidFireQAs.q: 58M + loses consciousness while shaving + tilt-table test shows no abnormalities; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: NBME wants “carotid sinus hypersensitivity” as answer. If tilt-table test (+), answer = vasovagal syncope.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + fundoscopy shows hard exudates + cotton wool spots + scattered hemorrhages; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: diabetic retinopathy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Medication that can cause tardive dyskinesia that is not an antipsychotic?
rapidFireQAs.a: metoclopramide (D2 antagonist); can also prolong QT interval and cause hyperprolactinemia.

rapidFireQAs.q: Anti-depressant med causing seizures?
rapidFireQAs.a: bupropion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 56M + 3-day Hx of cutting from 12 beers a day down to 4; develops tremulousness; Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chlordiazepoxide (delirium tremens); classic vignette is guy has surgery + two days later has tachycardia, tremulousness, and hallucinations (alcoholic hallucinosis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + high ESR and creatine kinase (CK) + proximal muscle weakness +/- muscle pain; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: polymyositis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + high ESR + no mention of high CK or weakness in the vignette + muscle pain + muscle stiffness; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR).

rapidFireQAs.q: 59F + temporal headache + muscle pain and stiffness + high ESR; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: temporal arteritis + polymyalgia rheumatica → next best step? = IV methylprednisolone first, followed by temporal artery biopsy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 68M + Hx of prostate cancer + now has neurologic findings; next best step in Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: MRI of spine to look for mets → however if corticosteroids are listed, choose these before MRI → for spinal cord compression on NBME (from cancer or trauma), choose steroids first if listed.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65F + breast cancer + neurologic findings; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Neuro NBME is “intravenous high-dose dexamethasone.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + prostate cancer + neurologic findings; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “epidural spinal cord compression” due to spinal mets → do steroids first (if listed), then MRI.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient has brain cancer; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: steroids.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx brain cancer?
rapidFireQAs.a: contrast head CT (done for cancer and abscess).

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx brain bleed?
rapidFireQAs.a: non-contrast CT (always done for intracranial bleeds).

rapidFireQAs.q: Epidural hematoma; next best step after CT confirms?
rapidFireQAs.a: intubation and hyperventilation on Neuro NBME. After this is done, craniotomy is the answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: Subdural hematoma; next best step after CT?
rapidFireQAs.a: craniotomy on NBME, not observation.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do you see on non-contrast CT with epidural vs subdural?
rapidFireQAs.a: epidural hematoma = lens-shaped bleed; subdural = crescent-shaped.

rapidFireQAs.q: BP of 220/120 + sodium nitroprusside administered; now patient has confusion; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cyanide toxicity caused by nitroprusside.

rapidFireQAs.q: Drug that can be given to prevent vasospasm after a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)?
rapidFireQAs.a: nimodipine (dihydropyridine CCB).

rapidFireQAs.q: Severe headache + stiff neck; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: SAH (can cause meningism, similar to meningitis).

rapidFireQAs.q: Brain bleed in patient with Alzheimer; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: amyloid angiopathy (intracerebral hemorrhage).

rapidFireQAs.q: 87F + Alzheimer + low-grade fever + delirium; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: do urinalysis to look for UTI as cause of delirium.

rapidFireQAs.q: Viral infection + tinnitus + vertigo +/- neurosensory hearing loss
rapidFireQAs.a: labyrinthitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Viral infection + vertigo
rapidFireQAs.a: vestibular neuritis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for acute flare of MS
rapidFireQAs.a: IV steroids (oral is wrong and can make flares worse).

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx between flares of MS (the patient must by asymptomatic)
rapidFireQAs.a: IFN-beta (interferon beta).

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for spasticity in MS
rapidFireQAs.a: baclofen (GABA-B receptor agonist).

rapidFireQAs.q: Incontinence in MS
rapidFireQAs.a: urge (hyperactive detrusor; detrusor instability).

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for MS?
rapidFireQAs.a: T cell-mediated attack against oligodendrocytes.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx MS?
rapidFireQAs.a: MRI is gold standard; choose MRI over CSF IgG oligoclonal bands.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + intermittent headaches + blurry vision; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: optic neuritis (multiple sclerosis) → student says “why the headaches?” Yeah, I know. Weird. But it’s on the NBME. You need to know optic neuritis is HY in MS and means inflammation of cranial nerve II → presents as blurry vision, or change in color vision, or Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect).

rapidFireQAs.q: Most specific eye finding in MS
rapidFireQAs.a: medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) syndrome → aka internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) → when you abduct to one side, you activate CN VI on that side, which requires the contralateral CN III to activate in order to adduct → the side that cannot adduct is the side that’s impaired; the normal side will have nystagmus.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to differentiate CN III lesion from INO?
rapidFireQAs.a: INO patients can converge normally.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20F + stiffness of hands + frontal balding + impaired relaxation of hypothenar muscles; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: myotonic dystrophy (CTG TNR disorder).

rapidFireQAs.q: Cancer patient on cisplatin or vincristine + develops neuropathy; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: toxic neuropathy (chemotherapy-induced neuropathy); these drugs are neurotoxic.

rapidFireQAs.q: Confusion and/or seizure due to electrolyte disturbance; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypo-/hypernatremia and hypercalcemia all cause CNS dysfunction.

rapidFireQAs.q: Confusion in the setting of high BUN and creatinine; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: uremic encephalopathy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Floppy baby syndrome; Dx and location of CNS/PNS affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: Werdnig-Hoffmann syndrome (spinal muscular atrophy); anterior horns affected.

rapidFireQAs.q: Antipsychotic medication started + muscle rigidity + no fever; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: acute dystonia, not neuroleptic malignant syndrome (because no fever); Tx with benztropine (muscarinic receptor antagonist) or diphenhydramine (1st gen H1 blocker, which has strong anti-muscarinic side-effects).

rapidFireQAs.q: Antipsychotic medication started + abnormal eye movements + stiff neck; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: acute dystonia (oculogyric crisis + torticollis).

rapidFireQAs.q: Antipsychotic medication started + muscle rigidity + fever; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: neuroleptic malignant syndrome; give dantrolene (inhibits ryanodine channel).

rapidFireQAs.q: Antipsychotic med + restlessness; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: akathisia; Tx with propranolol.

rapidFireQAs.q: Antipsychotic med + bradykinesia; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: drug-induced Parkinsonism; Tx with amantadine or propranolol.

rapidFireQAs.q: Antipsychotic med + abnormal tongue movements; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: tardive dyskinesia; stop antipsychotic + switch to atypical.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for diabetic neuropathic pain?
rapidFireQAs.a: TCA (i.e., amitriptyline). Second-line is gabapentin

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for herpetic / post-herpetic neuralgia (i.e., from shingles)?
rapidFireQAs.a: gabapentin

rapidFireQAs.q: 82M diabetic + neuropathic pain + already taking carbamazepine + gabapentin to no avail; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: switch the meds to nortriptyline (a TCA) → student then asks, “Wait, I thought you said TCAs are first-line. Why does this Q have the guy on those two meds then?” → two points: 1) we don’t like giving TCAs to elderly because of their anticholinergic and anti-alpha-1 side-effects, so this vignette happen to try other agents first, but if you’re asked first-line, always choose TCA; and 2) if we do give a TCA to an elderly patient, we choose nortriptyline because it carries fewer adverse effects.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to differentiate cluster headache from trigeminal neuralgia?
rapidFireQAs.a: cluster will be a male 20s-40s with 11/10 lancinating pain behind the eye waking him up at night (he may pace around the room until it goes away); details such as lacrimation and rhinorrhea are too easy and will likely not show up on the shelf. In contrast, trigeminal neuralgia will be 11/10 lancinating pain behind the eye (or along the cheek / jaw if V2 or V3 branches affected; it’s when V1 is affected that this diagnoses are more readily confused) → TN is brought on by a minor stimulus such as brushing one’s hair or teeth, or a gust of wind.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx and prophylaxis for cluster headache?
rapidFireQAs.a: Tx = 100% oxygen; prophylaxis = verapamil.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx and prophylaxis for trigeminal neuralgia?
rapidFireQAs.a: Tx = goes away on its own because it lasts only seconds; prophylaxis = carbamazepine.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx and prophylaxis for migraine?
rapidFireQAs.a: Tx = NSAID, followed by triptan (triptans are NOT prophylaxis; they are for abortive therapy only after NSAIDs); prophylaxis = propranolol.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + diffuse headache relieved by acetaminophen + sleep; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: tension-type headache; Tx = rest + taper caffeine (if taking it).

rapidFireQAs.q: Other HY uses for propranolol?
rapidFireQAs.a: Migraine prophylaxis Akathisia (with antipsychotic use) Thyroid storm (decreases peripheral conversion of T4 to T3) Essential tremor (bilateral resting tremor in young adult; autosomal dominant; patient will self-medicate with EtOH, which decreases tremor). Hypertension + idiopathic tremor. Esophageal varices prophylaxis (patients at risk of bleeds) Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (increases preload → decreases murmur) Social phobia

rapidFireQAs.q: 47M + bitemporal hemianopsia; most likely tumor?
rapidFireQAs.a: prolactinoma (most common pituitary tumor in adults).

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + bitemporal hemianopsia; most likely tumor?
rapidFireQAs.a: craniopharyngioma (most common pituitary tumor in children; some sources argue not true pituitary tumor because it’s derived from Rathke pouch, which is the roof of the primitive pharynx).

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common primary brain cancer in children?
rapidFireQAs.a: pilocytic astrocytoma → solid + cystic on MRI; has Rosenthal fibers → not aggressive.

rapidFireQAs.q: 3F + morning vomiting + truncal ataxia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: medulloblastoma of cerebellar vermis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common primary brain cancer in adults?
rapidFireQAs.a: glioblastoma multiforme (butterfly glioma) → areas of necrosis + hemorrhage (large, irregular mass on head CT); often presents with seizure.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + SLE + irregular ring-enhancing lesion seen on head CT; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: primary CNS lymphoma, not Toxo.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate + intracranial calcifications + chorioretinitis + hydrocephalus; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Congenital Toxo.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate + intracranial calcifications + deafness + hepatomegaly + rash; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: CMV.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate with bilateral deafness due to maternal infection + no other info given; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: congenital CMV.

rapidFireQAs.q: CNS tumors seen in neurofibromatosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: oligodendroglioma + ependymoma + optic nerve glioma in NF1; in NF2, meningioma. These may overlap, but be aware that these tumors can merely occur in either NF, period.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + jaw pain + headaches + normal ESR; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: temporal mandibular joint syndrome; if ESR is high, answer is jaw claudication caused by temporal arteritis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F being treated for TB + has neurologic findings in extremities +/- seizure; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency caused by isoniazid.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65F + metastatic breast cancer + suprapubic mass + decreased sphincter tone + pain over lumbar vertebrae on fist percussion; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: metastases to cauda equina.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + saddle anesthesia + late urinary incontinence; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cauda equina syndrome → bundle of spinal nerves and rootlets arising from the conus medullaris).

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + perianal anesthesia + early urinary + fecal incontinence; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: conus medullaris syndrome → bulbous end of the spinal cord = conus medullaris.

rapidFireQAs.q: 48M + burns his thumb; pain sensed via which dermatome?
rapidFireQAs.a: C6; lateral digits primarily C6; middle finger C7; medial digits primarily C8.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does CSF show in GBS?
rapidFireQAs.a: albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein but normal cells).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + weakness proximally and distally in lower limbs + weakness distally in upper limbs; rest of the vignette is vague; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: GBS → this descriptor means paralysis/paresis has ascending in lower limbs but not yet in upper limbs.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism of GBS?
rapidFireQAs.a: T cell attack against Schwann cells of PNS.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of GBS?
rapidFireQAs.a: IVIG + plasmapheresis; steroids are the wrong answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + paresthesias in thenar region of hand +/- hand weakness + sensation intact over dorsum of hand; next best step in Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Neuro NBME exam wants “Electrophysiological testing.” it’s what they want. Examination findings such as Tinel sign, Phalen maneuver, Flick test are insufficient for diagnosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: First Tx for carpal tunnel syndrome in patient who can’t stop offending activity (e.g., office worker)
rapidFireQAs.a: wrist splint first; then triamcinolone (steroid) injection into the carpal tunnel; do not select anything surgical as it’s always wrong on the USMLE; NSAIDs are a wrong answer and not proven to help

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for cubital tunnel syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: elbow splint.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is cubital tunnel syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: ulnar nerve entrapment at elbow → presents similarly to carpal tunnel syndrome but just in an ulnar distribution and involves the forearm.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is Guyon canal syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist → hook of hamate fracture or chronic handle bar impaction in avid cyclists.

rapidFireQAs.q: Midshaft fracture of humerus; which nerve is injured?
rapidFireQAs.a: radial → wrist-drop + pronated forearm.

rapidFireQAs.q: Supracondylar fracture of humerus; which nerve is injured?
rapidFireQAs.a: median.

rapidFireQAs.q: Medial epicondylar fracture; nerve injury?
rapidFireQAs.a: ulnar.

rapidFireQAs.q: Surgical neck of humerus fracture; nerve injury?
rapidFireQAs.a: axillary.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mastectomy + post-operative winged scapula; nerve injury?
rapidFireQAs.a: long thoracic nerve.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which muscle is innervated by long thoracic nerve?
rapidFireQAs.a: serratus anterior.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + ECG shows miscellaneous arrhythmia + seizure-like episode; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Adam-Stokes attack → not true seizure disorder as per EEG; arrythmia leads to hypoxia of brainstem → seizure-like fits ensue.

rapidFireQAs.q: 75M + episodes of loss of consciousness (LoC) for 2 years + tonic-clonic-like episodes + becomes pale and sweaty + Hx of MI; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “syncope” on the NBME (convulsive syncope).

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism of narcolepsy?
rapidFireQAs.a: deficiency of orexin (hypocretin).

rapidFireQAs.q: Diagnosis of narcolepsy?
rapidFireQAs.a: polysomnography.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is cataplexy?
rapidFireQAs.a: loss of muscle tone usually in response to emotional stimulus (e.g., laughter) → seen in narcolepsy.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is simple vs complex seizure?
rapidFireQAs.a: simple = no LoC; complex = LoC; patient staring off into space not aware of surroundings = LoC.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is partial vs generalized seizure?
rapidFireQAs.a: partial = affecting one part of the brain; generalized = involves the wholes of both cerebral hemispheres.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is myoclonic seizure?
rapidFireQAs.a: jerks in muscle or group of muscles; no LoC.

rapidFireQAs.q: Empiric Abx therapy for meningitis
rapidFireQAs.a: ceftriaxone + vancomycin (+/- steroids).

rapidFireQAs.q: Lumbar puncture or Abx first in suspected meningitis?
rapidFireQAs.a: new guidelines say LP first.

rapidFireQAs.q: When do you do CT head before LP in suspected meningitis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Confusion that interferes with neurologic exam / decreased GCS score. Seizure. Focal neurologic signs (motor or sensory). Papilledema or if the optic fundi cannot be visualized. Above reasons indicate potential mass lesion, where if you do an LP you can cause tonsillar herniation and death; if CT negative, proceed cautiously to LP.

rapidFireQAs.q: Herpes encephalitis: lots of RBCs in CSF due to temporal lobe hemorrhage
rapidFireQAs.a: CT is often negative, but sometimes Q will mention wave slowing or temporal complexes on EEG. Tx = IV acyclovir.

rapidFireQAs.q: Difference between meningitis and encephalitis
rapidFireQAs.a: meningitis is nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness) + photophobia + ophthalmoplegia; encephalitis presents with confusion.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of Cryptococcal meningitis?
rapidFireQAs.a: latex agglutination if it’s listed over India ink; mucicarmine staining (red stain) can also be done.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for Cryptococcal meningitis
rapidFireQAs.a: amphotericin B + flucytosine, followed by fluconazole taper.

rapidFireQAs.q: Nodular density in upper lobe in immunocompromised pt
rapidFireQAs.a: aspergilloma → next best step = open lung biopsy (sounds radical, but it’s the answer on one of the NBME forms) → Tx with -azole → invasive aspergillosis can be treated with caspofungin or voriconazole.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + diplopia + dysphagia + eyelid ptosis; all worsen throughout the day; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: myasthenia gravis (MG).

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + proximal muscle weakness + able to perform upward gaze without a problem for 60 seconds; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Lambert-Eaton (LE) syndrome (if cannot perform, answer = MG).

rapidFireQAs.q: Vignette where Dx is either MG or LE but it’s not listed; answer?
rapidFireQAs.a: “neuromuscular junction.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + difficulty getting up from chair but is able to after several attempts; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: LE.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism of MG vs LE?
rapidFireQAs.a: MG = antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors; LE = antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.

rapidFireQAs.q: MG can sometimes be paraneoplastic syndromes of which cancer?
rapidFireQAs.a: MG from thymoma (do chest imaging to check for thymoma after Dx of MG; if thymoma present + removed, this cures the MG). Up to 80% of patients with thymoma + MG have anti-MUSK Abs (muscle-specific kinase).

rapidFireQAs.q: LE can sometimes be a paraneoplastic syndrome of which cancer?
rapidFireQAs.a: small cell lung cancer.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx MG vs LE?
rapidFireQAs.a: If both are listed, choose antibodies over Tensilon (edrophonium) test.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is edrophonium
rapidFireQAs.a: short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.

rapidFireQAs.q: How do MG vs LE perform with edrophonium?
rapidFireQAs.a: MG improves drastically; LE less change.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of MG?
rapidFireQAs.a: give an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (i.e., pyridostigmine).

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + dancing eyes + HTN + lesion visualized in posterior mediastinum on CXR; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: neuroblastoma; students says ? → can occur anywhere in the median sympathetic chain, although classically intra- abdominal. Dancing eyes = opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neuroblastoma; how to Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on NBME is “urinary homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA); mIBG scan may also be used; n-myc gene.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + impaired plantar flexion + inversion; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: tibial nerve injury.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + impaired dorsiflexion + eversion; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: common peroneal nerve injury.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F returns from Central America + has tonic-clonic seizure + CT of head shows “swiss cheese” appearance of brain, or cystic structures in ventricles, or white specs somewhat diffusely (I’ve seen all three images on NBME forms); Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium); Tx = albendazole (or praziquantel).

rapidFireQAs.q: AIDS patient with CD4 count of 47/uL + cognitive degeneration + miscellaneous peripheral neurologic findings; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by JC polyoma virus; USMLE wants “reactivation of latent infection”; “acute infection in immunocompromised patient” is the wrong answer. T2-weighted MRI shows multiple hyperintensities.

rapidFireQAs.q: 55F + few-month Hx of spinning sensation + no vomiting + when head hangs off examination table she develops coarse, rotary nystagmus beating to one side; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on NBME is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BBPV); need not be associated with vomiting; Dx with Dix-Hallpike maneuver; Tx with Epley maneuver.

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of BPPV?
rapidFireQAs.a: posterior semicircular canal otolith.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is cholesteatoma?
rapidFireQAs.a: non-cancerous squamous proliferation of middle ear.

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of carotid plaques?
rapidFireQAs.a: HTN → the strong systolic impulse from the heart pounds the carotids --> endothelial damage --> atherosclerosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: What % of people over age 80 have AF?
rapidFireQAs.a: 8% of people over age 80 have AF, which is why age is a huge risk factor. In other words, if the vignette says the guy is 58, AF is probably less likely just based on shear probability, regardless of hypertensive status." And, once again, knowing that AF is often paroxysmal is really important.

rapidFireQAs.q: Age 50s-60s + high BP + TIA/stroke/retinal artery occlusion; next best step in Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: carotid duplex ultrasound to look for carotid plaques.

rapidFireQAs.q: Age >75 + good BP + TIA/stroke/retinal artery occlusion; answer = ECG to look for AF
rapidFireQAs.a: if normal, do Holter monitor to pick up paroxysmal AF.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Mx carotid plaques?
rapidFireQAs.a: first we have to ask whether the patient is symptomatic or asymptomatic. A bruit does not count as symptoms (that's a sign). Symptomatic means stroke, TIA, or retinal artery occlusion. According to recent guidelines: carotid occlusion >70% if symptomatic, or >80% if asymptomatic → answer = do carotid endarterectomy. Below these thresholds → answer = medical management = statin, PLUS clopidogrel OR dipyridamole + aspirin. The USMLE will actually not be hyper-pedantic about the occlusion %s (that’s Qbank). They'll make it obvious for you which answer they want. They'll say either 90% → answer certainly = carotid endarterectomy, or they'll say 50% → answer = medical management only. There’s one NBME Q where they say a guy has a bruit but is asymptomatic, and has 10 and 30% occlusion in the left vs right carotids, respectively, and he’s already on aspirin + statin, and the answer is "maintain current regimen” → if he were symptomatic, even with low occlusion, he’d certainly need statin, PLUS clopidogrel OR dipyridamole + aspirin.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6F + rheumatic fever + has Sydenham chorea; Q asks mechanism
rapidFireQAs.a: autoimmune disorder to the basal ganglia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 38F + hoarseness of voice + various stress factors; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: conversion disorder; merely be aware that hoarseness of voice is assessed for this.

rapidFireQAs.q: Back pain worse when standing or walking for long periods of time
rapidFireQAs.a: lumbar spinal stenosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Radiculopathy down an arm
rapidFireQAs.a: cervical disc herniation.

rapidFireQAs.q: Bilateral paresthesias in the arms in rheumatoid arthritis patient
rapidFireQAs.a: atlantoaxial subluxation.

rapidFireQAs.q: Bilateral paresthesias in the arms in rheumatoid arthritis patient
rapidFireQAs.a: MRI of spine to Dx atlantoaxial subluxation.

rapidFireQAs.q: Prior to surgery in rheumatoid arthritis patient
rapidFireQAs.a: cervical CT or flexion/extension x-rays of cervical spine to check for atlantoaxial subluxation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + combination of LMN and UMN findings + no sensory abnormalities; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; make sure you memorize that there are NO sensory findings, as this is the detail most students forget. Sometimes the answer won’t be “ALS,” but will instead be “motor neuron” (i.e., they’ll ask for structural diagnosis, rather than disease name).

rapidFireQAs.q: 1-year-old boy + hypotonia + honey consumption; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ingestion of spores (honey); botulism (Clostridium botulinum).

rapidFireQAs.q: 13M + camping trip + Bell palsy + constipation + hypotonia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ingestion of preformed toxin from compromised canned goods. Tx = anti-toxin.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + waxing and waning tinnitus and hearing loss + difficulty hearing conversations at dinner and in groups + has family Hx of similar Sx; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Meniere disease → low-frequency hearing loss.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for Meniere?
rapidFireQAs.a: defective endolymphatic drainage; may attempt antihistamines and diuretics.

rapidFireQAs.q: Viral infection + tinnitus +/- vertigo + no hearing loss; self-resolves over weeks to months; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: vestibular neuritis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Viral infection + tinnitus + hearing loss +/- vertigo self-resolves over weeks to months; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: labyrinthitis. One Q on the neuro forms has presentation similar to vestibular neuritis but answer is labyrinthitis; vestibular neuritis isn’t listed as alternative answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + pinna displaced upward and outward + fever; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: mastoiditis (malignant otitis externa).

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M IV drug user + Tx for endocarditis + now the room is spinning; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: CN VIII toxicity caused by aminoglycoside (can be hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo); empiric endocarditis Tx is usually gentamicin + either vancomycin or ampicillin/sulbactam.

rapidFireQAs.q: Endocarditis patient + has stroke-like episode + fever; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: IV antibiotics → septic embolus to the brain; can lead to brain abscess.

rapidFireQAs.q: MCA stroke on dominant hemisphere (usually left-sided); HY findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: contralateral limb + face sensory and/or motor deficits; also classically associated with Broca and Wernicke aphasias.

rapidFireQAs.q: ACA stroke; HY findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: contralateral lower leg sensory and/or motor dysfunction.

rapidFireQAs.q: PCA stroke; HY findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: contralateral hemianopsia with macular sparing.

rapidFireQAs.q: Broca aphasia; HY findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: non-fluent aphasia; telegraphic speech; comprehends normally but cannot communicate easily, leading to frustration; repetition impaired.

rapidFireQAs.q: Where is Broca area?
rapidFireQAs.a: posterior, lateral, inferior frontal lobe.

rapidFireQAs.q: Wernicke aphasia; HY findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: fluent aphasia; word salad; non-sensical speech + does not comprehend; repetition impaired.

rapidFireQAs.q: Where is Wernicke area?
rapidFireQAs.a: superior temporal gyrus (temporal lobe).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is conduction aphasia?
rapidFireQAs.a: patient has only impaired repetition (arcuate fasciculus connecting Broca and Wernicke areas).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is global aphasia?
rapidFireQAs.a: patient has presentation of Broca and Wernicke aphasias at the same time.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is transcortical motor aphasia?
rapidFireQAs.a: patient sounds like he/she has Broca aphasia but repetition is intact.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is transcortical sensory aphasia?
rapidFireQAs.a: patient sounds like he/she has Wernicke aphasia but repetition is intact.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is mixed transcortical aphasia?
rapidFireQAs.a: patient sounds like he/she has Broca and Wernicke at the same time but repetition is intact.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42M + acalculia + left-right agnosia + finger agnosia + agraphia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Gerstmann syndrome (angular gyrus syndrome; junction of parietal and temporal lobes).

rapidFireQAs.q: Stroke causing Horner syndrome + dysphagia + loss of pain/temp from contralateral body and ipsilateral face; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: lateral medullary syndrome (PICA infarct) → “Pikachu” = PICA-chew = dysphagia with PICA infarct.

rapidFireQAs.q: Stroke causing ipsilateral Bell palsy; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: lateral pontine syndrome (AICA infarct) → FACIAL spelled backwards has AICA in it → face is affected.

rapidFireQAs.q: Stroke causing ipsilateral tongue deviation + contralateral paralysis and loss of propioception; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: medial medullary syndrome (paramedian branch of anterior spinal artery).

rapidFireQAs.q: Lacunar infarct HY points?
rapidFireQAs.a: caused by HTN leading to lipohyalinosis of lenticulostriate vessels → if affecting posterior limb of internal capsule, deficits are pure motor (contralateral); if thalamic, deficits are pure sensory (contralateral).

rapidFireQAs.q: Stroke causing locked-in syndrome; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Basilar artery stroke.

rapidFireQAs.q: Correct hyponatremia too quickly?
rapidFireQAs.a: locked-in syndrome due to central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination).

rapidFireQAs.q: Correct hypernatremia too quickly?
rapidFireQAs.a: cerebral edema.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pain in contralateral limb months after stroke resolves; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: thalamic pain syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: Coma or persistent vegetative state following deceleration injury (i.e., MVA or fall); Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: diffuse axonal injury.

rapidFireQAs.q: 10-month old boy + jerking movements of the limbs + EEG shows chaotic high-amplitude spikes with no recognizable pattern; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: West syndrome (infantile spasms) → triad of spasms + hypsarrhythmia on EEG (no recognizable pattern with high amplitude spikes) + developmental regression; international definition of the diagnosis requires two out of three; starts age 3-12 months; seen in 1-5% of Down syndrome kids; Tx = ACTH, prednisolone, or vigabatrin; ACTH is thought to act by two mechanisms: 1) stimulates steroid (cortisol) release; 2) direct (cortisol-independent) effect on melanocortin receptors.

rapidFireQAs.q: 13M + tonic-clonic seizure + 4-month Hx of hypnagogic/hypnopompic jerking of left arm + uncle has epilepsy; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; genetic with unclear inheritance pattern; characterized by myoclonic jerks (usually hypnagogic and/or hypnopompic) that progress to tonic- clonic seizures after several months; age of onset is usually 10-16, but can also start in adulthood; Tx is valproic acid.

rapidFireQAs.q: 4F + few-month Hx of near-daily seizures + seizures typically occur while she’s sleeping + has started putting objects in her mouth and making less eye contact + seizures not responding to anti-epileptic meds; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome → severe childhood-onset epilepsy characterized by near-daily seizures and cognitive decline (hyperoralism is a sign of cognitive regression [babies put things in their mouths]); poor prognosis, with 5% mortality rate in childhood; 80-90% persistence of seizures into adulthood. HY NEURO

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + long-standing Hx of seizures + the following picture represents her condition; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: arteriovenous malformation (AVM) → looks almost like swiss cheese. This is a HY image for Step 1.

rapidFireQAs.q: 82M + long-standing HTN + weakness of right arm and right side of face; occlusion of which vessel is responsible for patient’s presentation?
rapidFireQAs.a: left middle cerebral artery (MCA) → MCA strokes will cause deficits of contralateral upper limb and face; Hx of HTN suggests carotid atherosclerosis with a plaque launching off to the circle of Willis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 74F + atrial fibrillation + weakness of left leg; occlusion of which vessel is responsible for patient’s presentation?
rapidFireQAs.a: right anterior cerebral artery (ACA) → ACA strokes will cause deficits of contralateral lower limb; Hx of AF suggests left atrial mural thrombus launched off to circle of Willis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 66M + HTN + weakness of left arm; where is the stroke lesion? (answer the following three Qs)
rapidFireQAs.a: 1) left or right side of the brain? → answer = right (contralateral). 2) medial or lateral cerebral hemisphere? → answer = lateral (homunculus for upper limb and face is lateral; leg is medial). 3) anterior or posterior to the central sulcus? → answer = anterior (primary motor cortex is anterior; primary sensory is posterior).

rapidFireQAs.q: 92F + atrial fibrillation + numbness/tingling of her right leg; where is the stroke lesion?
rapidFireQAs.a: 1) left or right side of the brain? → answer = left (contralateral). 2) medial or lateral cerebral hemisphere? → answer = medial (homunculus for lower limb is medial; upper limb and face are lateral). 3) anterior or posterior to the central sulcus? → answer = posterior (primary sensory cortex is posterior; primary motor is anterior).

rapidFireQAs.q: 66M + chronic HTN managed with lisinopril + paresthesias of left leg; using the following diagram, which letter corresponds to the part of the brain that is affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: F → stroke affects left side of body, is sensory, and is lower limb, so we know that the lesion must be contralateral (i.e., we can eliminate A-D, which are the left side of the brain; i.e., the stroke must be on the right side of the brain), medial (lower limb is medial brain as per the homunculus; upper limb and face are lateral brain), and posterior to the central sulcus (primary sensory cortex is posterior; primary motor cortex is anterior).

rapidFireQAs.q: Using the above image, describe how each letter corresponds to a stroke in terms of 1) side of the body affected, 2) sensory vs motor, and 3) upper limb/face vs lower limb:
rapidFireQAs.a: A → Motor disturbance (i.e., paresis/paralysis) of right arm + face. B → Sensory disturbance (i.e., numbness, paresthesias, pain) of right arm + face. C → Motor; right leg. D → Sensory; right leg. E → Motor; left leg. F → Sensory; left leg. G → Motor; left arm + face. H → Sensory; left arm + face.

rapidFireQAs.q: 91M + Hx of atrial fibrillation + new-onset difficulty articulating speech (i.e., words come out “telegraphic”); repetition is impaired; comprehension is intact; where on the following diagram is affected? Also describe what lesions of the other letters would result in:
rapidFireQAs.a: A (Broca area; inferior frontal gyrus; frontal lobe) → Broca aphasia → non-fluent aphasia with repetition impaired; patient comprehends without a problem and appears frustrated with inability to articulate fluently. Choice B (primary auditory cortex) → not HY, but labeled nevertheless because NBME Q might show you this lettered distribution and can be hard to distinguish B from C. Choice C (Wernicke area; superior temporal gyrus; temporal lobe) → Wernicke aphasia → fluent aphasia with repetition impaired → “word salad,” where patient can articulate without issue but makes no sense; also cannot comprehend. Choice D (angular gyrus; parietal lobe) → transfers information to Wernicke area; lesion causes Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, right-left agnosia, finger agnosia, acalculia; not an overwhelmingly HY diagnosis, but students tend to carry an infatuation with it nevertheless. Choice E (supramarginal gyrus) → not HY, but labeled nevertheless because NBME Q might show you this lettered distribution; thought to play a role in empathy and interpreting people’s gestures. Choice F (arcuate fasciculus) → conduction aphasia → impaired repetition only. If stroke sounds like Broca but repetition not impaired, Dx? → answer = transcortical motor aphasia. If stroke sounds like Wernicke but repetition not impaired; Dx? → answer = transcortical sensory aphasia. If stroke sounds like both Broca + Wernicke at the same time but repetition not impaired, Dx? → answer = mixed transcortical aphasia. If stroke sounds like both Broca + Wernicke at the same time and repetition is impaired; Dx? → answer = global aphasia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + Broca aphasia; which vessel is affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: left MCA (always assume left brain is dominant, unless Q specifically explicates the patient is left-handed).

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + Wernicke aphasia; which vessel is affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: left MCA (same).

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + Broca aphasia; where in the brain is affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: inferior frontal gyrus of frontal lobe (reiterating this because of yieldness for Step 1).

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + Wernicke aphasia; where in the brain is affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: superior temporal gyrus of temporal lobe (reiterating this because of yieldness for Step 1).

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + cannot draw clockface properly; Dx + where is the stroke?
rapidFireQAs.a: hemineglect syndrome caused by stroke in non-dominant parietal lobe (i.e., right MCA in most people) → leads to neglect of left visual field, although the patient can still see perfectly fine; hemineglect usually affects left visual field (i.e., left clockface) because most brains are left-, not right-, dominant; hemineglect of the right visual field is rare because of redundant processing.

rapidFireQAs.q: Identify:
rapidFireQAs.a: A = Broca area; B = premotor cortex; C = primary motor cortex; D = primary sensory cortex; E = primary auditory cortex; F = Wernicke area; G = occipital pole of occipital lobe.

rapidFireQAs.q: Identify:
rapidFireQAs.a: A = frontal lobe; B = medial premotor cortex; the answer if the vignette mentions the patient planning on making a movement of his left leg. C = medial primary motor cortex (pre-central gyrus); the answer if post-stroke patient has weakness of the left leg. D = medial primary sensory cortex (post-central gyrus); the answer if the post-stroke patient has sensory disturbance (i.e., paresthesias, numbness) of the left leg. E = corpus collosum; F = thalamus; G = midbrain; H = pons; I = medulla. J = cerebellar vermis; the answer if patient has truncal ataxia. K = posterior lobe of cerebellum; the answer if the patient has right limb ataxia (ipsilateral for cerebellar lesions).

rapidFireQAs.q: Identify:
rapidFireQAs.a: L = somatosensory association area; integrates information received from the primary sensory cortex (lies just posterior to primary sensory cortex). M = lateral primary sensory cortex (post-central gyrus); the answer if the post-stroke patient has sensory disturbance (i.e., paresthesias, numbness) of the left arm and face. N = central sulcus. O = lateral primary motor cortex (pre-central gyrus); the answer if post-stroke patient has weakness of the left arm and face. P = medial premotor cortex; the answer when planning on moving the left leg. Q = frontal lobe; the answer for post-stroke patient with apathy, disinhibition, and personality change. R = superior temporal gyrus of non-dominant hemisphere (in most people, the left superior temporal gyrus is dominant and contains the primary auditory cortex and Wernicke area). S = lateral premotor cortex; the answer when planning on moving the left arm + face.

rapidFireQAs.q: Now identify:
rapidFireQAs.a: Frontal lobe shown in blue because of its high yieldness. In other words, the USMLE will show you a gross specimen without the cerebellum, where it can be difficult to tell which side is the frontal lobe. Therefore, recognizing the olfactory bulbs/tracts and saying “Ok, that’s the frontal lobe” is really important.

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + progressive personality change + apathy + pulls pants down when guests come over to the house; where on the following specimen is most likely the location of the pathology in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: L (frontal lobe); Dx = frontotemporal dementia (classically apathy, disinhibition, personality change).

rapidFireQAs.q: 69F + Hx of HTN + stroke + tongue deviated to left side; which of the following letters corresponds on the stroke lesion?
rapidFireQAs.a: Most students: “ am I looking at?” Yeah I get, but stick with me here. Answer = A → medial medullary syndrome. The NBMEs for Step 1 are littered with these types of cross- sections. You do not need to know every structure labeled on a cross-section. Waste of your time. You merely need to know that ipsilateral tongue deviation = medial medullary syndrome. So if tongue deviation is to the left, you say, “Ok, well that must be medial medulla of the same side, so I’ll just choose the letter on the left side of the cross-section that is most medial.” This is supplied by the paramedian branch of the anterior spinal artery (ASA). § In short: if tongue deviation in vignette; answer = medial medulla of ipsilateral side. Choice B refers to lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) → patient will have three main features: hoarseness of voice + dysphagia +/- Horner syndrome. You might say, “Wait, I thought Horner syndrome was for Pancoast tumor of the lung.” Yeah, but it’s also sometimes seen in lateral medullary syndrome. This is a huge giveaway if you get it in the vignette. You can also remember “PICACHEW” (Pikachu from Pokemon) → PICA → posterior inferior cerebellar artery is affected + CHEW → dysphagia. If PICA not listed, choose vertebral artery. § In short: if hoarseness/dysphagia +/- Horner in vignette, answer = lateral medulla of ipsilateral side.

rapidFireQAs.q: How the medulla cross-sections tend to appear on the Step 1 NBME/USMLE:
rapidFireQAs.a: If you get these types of slices on your exam and are deer in the headlights (i.e., you have no idea what you’re looking at), just remember: pay attention to whether they give you tongue deviation versus hoarseness/dysphagia +/- Horner; for tongue deviation, just choose the ipsilateral medial part of whichever slice they give you; for hoarseness/dysphagia +/- Horner, just choose ipsilateral lateral part of whichever slice they give you. No need to memorize 50 random structures.

rapidFireQAs.q: 70M + Hx of HTN + left-sided Bell’s palsy + left-sided hearing loss + loss of temperature/pain to left side of face and right side of body; which of the following letters corresponds to the stroke lesion?
rapidFireQAs.a: B → lateral pontine syndrome → classically causes ipsilateral Bell’s palsy +/- hearing loss; the Bells palsy is literally the key detail you need to know. Caused by lesion of anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) → mnemonic is FACIAL (Face is affected, and the word FACIAL contains AICA backwards). Choice A = medial pontine syndrome; for some reason lower yield compared to the aforementioned brainstem lesions, but be aware that it can cause abducens nerve palsy, so patient can have esotropia (medially directed eye). Bottom line is: if you get a question where it’s a stroke of some kind and the patient has Bell’s palsy, just choose the lateral letter on the ipsilateral side of the pons slice.

rapidFireQAs.q: Looking at the following CT of the pons, what’s the diagnosis; and what was the most likely cause?
rapidFireQAs.a: Diagnosis is central pontine myelinolysis secondary to correction of hyponatremia too rapidly with hypertonic saline; the patient will present with locked-in syndrome (inability to move entire body except for eye muscles; described as triad of quadriplegia + aphonia + impaired horizontal eye movements); do not confuse this with cerebral edema caused by correcting hypernatremia too quickly with hypotonic saline.

rapidFireQAs.q: Identify:
rapidFireQAs.a: A = crus cerebri; B = CN III (oculomotor) nucleus; C = cerebral aqueduct; D = substantia nigra. HY point: crus cerebri lesions cause contralateral spastic paralysis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 78M + Hx of HTN + left eye is directed laterally and inferiorly + weakness of right side of the body; Dx? → NBME answer = Weber syndrome → midbrain lesion resulting in ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CNIII) palsy + contralateral hemiparesis (loss of crus cerebri); lesion in paramedian branch of posterior cerebral artery (PCA).
rapidFireQAs.a: Bottom line is: if the vignette gives you a stroke syndrome of some kind where there’s oculomotor nerve palsy, choose Weber syndrome (midbrain lesion).

rapidFireQAs.q: 75F + many years ago had cerebral infarction + brain on autopsy appears as follows; what would her main deficit have been?
rapidFireQAs.a: spastic paralysis on the left side of the body (right crus cerebri infarcted).

rapidFireQAs.q: Identify:
rapidFireQAs.a: A = right inferior colliculus; B = right pyramidal tract; C = right medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF); D = left MLF; E = left pyramidal tract; F = left inferior colliculus. The inferior colliculi are part of the auditory system and play a role in sound processing. The MLF are the answer in multiple sclerosis when the patient cannot adduct one eye while abducting the other – for instance, choice D would be the answer if the patient cannot adduct the left eye while abducting the right; the right eye would exhibit nystagmus.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + one-week Hx of urge to run to the bathroom at inopportune moments + physical exam shows inability to adduct left eye when gazing to the right + convergence of gaze not affected; where on the following diagram represents the location of the pathology in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: D; diagnosis is medial longitudinal fasciculus syndrome (MLF syndrome; aka internuclear ophthalmoplegia; INO) in a patient with multiple sclerosis (vignette also describes urge incontinence); normal convergence tells us that CN III is intact bilaterally. What you need to know is this: in INO, the side that cannot adduct is the side of the pathology, so we know all letters on the patient’s right (A-C) are wrong; so looking at D-F, even if you have no idea, if you recognize the presentation as MLF syndrome, you can say, “Well, the name of the condition is medial longitudinal fasciculus syndrome, so I’ll just choose the letter that’s medial.” Mechanism for pathology: when you look to one side (let’s say the right), CN VI on the right and CN III on the left are activated. This unison of activation is accomplished when the left MLF is activated. In the case of MLF syndrome, the right eye can abduct without a problem, but the left eye will fail to adduct and the right eye will exhibit nystagmus back toward the midline. MLF syndrome is pathognomonic for multiple sclerosis. MS patients can also get optic neuritis (i.e., change in visual acuity, color vision, central scotoma, etc.), but this is not pathognomonic for MS (i.e., it can be seen in other circumstances, such as with ethambutol or sildenafil use). Exceedingly rare but MLF syndrome may occur in stroke due to HTN (still considered pathognomonic for MS).

rapidFireQAs.q: 74M + unilateral resting tremor + shuffling gait; where on the following MRI be represents the location of his pathology?
rapidFireQAs.a: D (midbrain); the substantia nigra pars compacta (blue) are located bilaterally within the midbrain:

rapidFireQAs.q: “Do I need to know the cranial nerves coming off the brainstem?”
rapidFireQAs.a: Yeah. NBME/USMLE will show you a brainstem specimen or drawing, and you need to be able to identify the nerve(s) they’re referring to:

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + hiking in Connecticut + circular rash on forearm + Bell’s palsy; which nerve on the following diagram explains her findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: facial nerve (choice H) → Bell’s palsy secondary to Lyme disease.

rapidFireQAs.q: 76M + stroke + uvula deviates to the left when he says “Ahh”; which letter on the following image is the most likely location of this patient’s pathology?
rapidFireQAs.a: right vagus nerve (choice E); uvula deviates to contralateral side; Choice A = right trochlear nerve; B = right facial nerve; C = right vestibulocochlear nerve; D = right glossopharyngeal nerve; F = left trigeminal nerve; G = left facial nerve; H = left vestibulocochlear nerve; I = left glossopharyngeal nerve; J = left vagus nerve. CRANIAL NERVE EXIT POINTS

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + complete loss of hearing in left ear; which CN is damaged?
rapidFireQAs.a: left vestibulocochlear.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which nerves enable the gag reflex?
rapidFireQAs.a: CN IX (afferent); CN X (efferent).

rapidFireQAs.q: 47M + touching the face just lateral to the nose produces pain; the nerve supplying this area of the face exits the skull through where?
rapidFireQAs.a: foramen rotundum (maxillary branch of trigeminal nerve).

rapidFireQAs.q: 19M + viral infection + Bell palsy; Q asks what other finding might be seen in this patient as a result of the nerve lesion
rapidFireQAs.a: right sided hyperacusis (loud sounds) → CN VII (facial) innervates stapedius muscle, which controls the stapes bone and functions to dampen sounds; lesion of CN VII can lead to hyperacusis in some patients.

rapidFireQAs.q: 48F + Hx of cystic kidneys + right pupil enlarged; an aneurysm of which of the following vessels might explain this presentation?
rapidFireQAs.a: posterior communicating artery (choice B); PCoM aneurysms can cause ipsilateral mydriasis (blown pupil); ↑ risk of ACoM and PCoM aneurysms in ADPKD; A = right internal carotid artery; C = posterior cerebral artery (PCA); D = frontal lobe; E = olfactory tract; F = basilar artery; G = posterior inferior cerebellar artery.

rapidFireQAs.q: 82F + Hx of atrial fibrillation + inability to move all muscles of body except for eyes; which of the letters on the following angiogram best reflects the location of the patient’s stroke?
rapidFireQAs.a: Angiogram is of the circle of Willis; answer = basilar artery stroke (choice F), resulting in locked-in syndrome; A = anterior cerebral artery (ACA); B = anterior communicating artery (ACoM); C = middle cerebral artery (MCA); D = internal carotid artery; E = posterior cerebral artery (PCA); G = vertebral artery.

rapidFireQAs.q: 68M + Hx of HTN + acute-onset painless loss of vision in the right eye; which letter on the following circle of Willis illustration best reflects the path of the patient’s embolus?
rapidFireQAs.a: D (ophthalmic artery); patient has central retinal artery occlusion from carotid plaque that launched off secondary to HTN; the retinal artery (aka central retinal artery) is a branch of the ophthalmic artery; A = anterior communicating artery (ACoM); B = anterior cerebral artery (ACA); C = middle cerebral artery (MCA); E = posterior communicating artery (PCoM); F = internal carotid artery; G = choroidal artery; H = posterior cerebral artery (PCA).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + Hx of fainting episodes + blood pressure lower in right arm than left arm; retrograde flow through which vessel in the following angiogram might be expected in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: right vertebral artery (choice D); diagnosis is subclavian steal syndrome (proximal stenosis of subclavian artery results in retrograde flow through the vertebral artery, which is the first branch of the subclavian). Choice A = right internal carotid artery; B = right external carotid artery; C = right common carotid artery; E = right subclavian artery; F = brachiocephalic artery; G = left internal carotid artery; H = left subclavian artery; I = left common carotid artery; J = aortic arch.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + boating accident + dysmetria of right side of body + normal strength; which letter on the following sagittal brain cross-section most likely corresponds to the site of her injury?
rapidFireQAs.a: cerebellar hemisphere (choice F; posterior lobe is labeled); cerebellar injuries cause ipsilateral dysmetria; choice E, in contrast, which is the cerebellar vermis, would cause truncal ataxia. Choice A = thalamus; B = midbrain; C = pons; D = medulla.

rapidFireQAs.q: 26M + has arm slashed in bar fight + presents with arm pronated and unable to extend wrist; which letter on the following image corresponds to this patient’s deficit? -
rapidFireQAs.a: radial nerve (choice C). A = musculocutaneous nerve; B = axillary nerve; D = median nerve; E = ulnar nerve. USMLE will ask you relatively easy presentation for a neurologic deficit but require you to identify where on the brachial plexus is affected. “What about spinal cord cross-sections?” → Know how following tracts course through the spinal cord:

rapidFireQAs.q: “Okay, but what do those tracts actually do?”
rapidFireQAs.a: Spinothalamic → pain and temperature. (HIGH YIELD) Dorsal columns → vibration + proprioception. (HIGH YIELD) Anterior + lateral corticospinal tracts → motor function. (HIGH YIELD)

rapidFireQAs.q: Choice A = dorsal horn; B = dorsal root; C = dorsal root ganglion; D = lateral horn; E = ventral horn; F = anterior white commissure; G = ventral root; H = spinal nerve.
rapidFireQAs.a: A = right corticospinal tract; B = right spinothalamic tract; C = right fasciculus cuneatus; D = right fasciculus gracilis; E = left fasciculus gracilis; F = left fasciculus cuneatus; G = left corticospinal tract; H = left spinothalamic tract. Fasciculus cuneatus → carries vibration/proprioception from the upper limbs + trunk. Fasciculus gracilis → carries vibration/proprioception from the lower limbs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + boating accident years prior to death + autopsy is performed in which a myelin stain is used; what was the most likely deficit in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: loss of vibration/proprioception of the lower limbs → there are bilateral lesions of the fasciculus gracilis of the dorsal columns (only white matter part of the spinal cord not stained black with the myelin stain, meaning it was demyelinated).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + viral infection + loss of left leg motor function + loss of left leg vibration/proprioception + loss of right leg pain/temperature sensation; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Brown-Sequard syndrome → hemisection of the spinal cord; classically stab wound, but can also be autoimmune (i.e., secondary to lupus myelitis or viral infection).

rapidFireQAs.q: 67M + long history of cervical spondylosis + whiplash injury after being rear-ended in MVA + weakness in upper limbs > weakness in lower limbs; Dx? → answer = central cord syndrome.
rapidFireQAs.a: Central cord syndrome is the answer when weakness in the upper limbs is greater than weakness in the lower limbs; typically follows hyperextension injury of the neck during whiplash in a rear-end MVA.

rapidFireQAs.q: 69M + long Hx of T2DM + bilateral loss of motor function and pain/temperature below level of nipples + intact vibration/proprioception; Dx? → answer = anterior cord syndrome (dorsal columns spared); often due to atherosclerosis + infarction of anterior spinal artery.
rapidFireQAs.a: Anterior cord syndrome is the answer when there’s preservation of vibration/proprioception but loss of motor + pain/temperature, classically in patient with arterial disease.

rapidFireQAs.q: Answer = tabes dorsalis
rapidFireQAs.a: neurosyphilis → loss of dorsal columns → dorsal columns are the only part not stained, reflective of demyelination → isolated loss of vibration/proprioception; motor function and pain/temperature sensation intact.

rapidFireQAs.q: 31M + motorcycle accident + presents with spinal lesion affecting the following area on the cross- section; what type of neurologic dysfunction is most likely in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: bilateral loss of pain and temperature; diagnosis is syringomyelia (lesion of anterior white commissure); can be due to trauma, infections, and classically Chiari I.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + unilateral restring tremor + increased hepatic ALT and AST + low hematocrit; which letter on the following MRI correctly labels this patient’s putamen?
rapidFireQAs.a: A = caudate nucleus; B = putamen; C = globus pallidus. Parkinsonism in a young patient is Wilson disease until proven otherwise; copper deposition can occur anywhere in the basal ganglia; the putamen is described as a classic location.

rapidFireQAs.q: 41M + one-year Hx of jerking movements of extremities + 6-month Hx of worsening dementia + father had similar presentation and died at age 56; where on the following MRI is the location of this patient’s pathology?
rapidFireQAs.a: The answer is the caudate nucleus, which is choice B. Choice A = anterior horn of lateral ventricle; C = internal capsule; D = putamen; E = third ventricle; F = thalamus.

rapidFireQAs.q: Identify:
rapidFireQAs.a: A = frontal lobe (medial frontal gyrus); B = frontal lobe (middle frontal gyrus); C = caudate nucleus; D = internal capsule; E = thalamus; F = occipital lobe (occipital pole).

rapidFireQAs.q: 78M + long Hx of HTN + sudden paresis of left side of his body; which letter on the following specimen is the most likely location of his stroke?
rapidFireQAs.a: The answer is C (posterior limb of internal capsule). A = anterior limb of internal capsule; B = genu of internal capsule. USMLE wants you to know that the lenticulostriate vessels supply the internal capsule. Chronic hypertension leads to lipohyalinosis and compromise of these vessels. Posterior limb infarcts can sometimes result in pure motor strokes with contralateral hemiparesis/-plegia. Lesions of posterior limb of internal capsule are sometimes described as causing “pure motor” dysfunction.

rapidFireQAs.q: 63M + longstanding Hx of HTN + acute-onset flailing movements of left arm; where on the following cross-section of the corpus striatum is the most likely location of the patient’s pathology? Answer = subthalamic nucleus (choice E); A
rapidFireQAs.a: hippocampus; B = crus cerebri; C = ventral medial nucleus of thalamus; D = substantia nigra; E = subthalamic nucleus; F = ventral lateral nucleus of thalamus.

rapidFireQAs.q: Identify:
rapidFireQAs.a: A = corpus collosum; B = thalamus; C = pituitary gland; D = medulla; E = clivus; F = cerebellum; G = pineal gland; H = superior sagittal sinus; I = torcular herophili.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + presents with hydrocephalus + MRI shows colloid cyst most likely located where on the following illustration?
rapidFireQAs.a: choice C (foramen of Monro); colloid cysts are almost always found originating from the roof of the anterior third ventricle, just posterior the foramen of Monro. Weirdly specific, but just be aware. A = frontal horn; B = third ventricle; D = temporal horn; E = lateral ventricles; F = aqueduct of Sylvius; G = fourth ventricle; H = occipital horn. Cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius → connects third and fourth ventricles. Foramen of Monro → connects the third ventricle to both lateral ventricles.

rapidFireQAs.q: Identify:
rapidFireQAs.a: A = lateral ventricles; B = colloid cyst of roof of the third ventricle; C = third ventricle. “How would the brain development stuff like diencephalon, mesencephalon, etc., be asked?” → First learn the following diagram:

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + unsteady gait + personality change + urinary incontinence + Parkinsonism; the enlarged structures labeled on the following CT are derived from which component of brain development (i.e., prosencephalon, diencephalon, etc.)?
rapidFireQAs.a: telencephalon of the prosencephalon → dilated lateral ventricles are seen in normal pressure hydrocephalus (wet, wobbly, wacky +/- Parkinsonism).

rapidFireQAs.q: 84M + one-year Hx of progressive cognitive decline + no Hx of HTN, CVD, or atrial fibrillation + experiences a stroke and dies; which of the following head CTs might best reflect this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: intracerebral (intraparenchymal) hemorrhage (choice D); Dx is amyloid angiopathy resulting in hemorrhagic stroke in Alzheimer disease; A = subdural hematoma; B = epidural hematoma; C = subarachnoid hemorrhage. Subdural hematoma (choice A) → rupture of bridging (superior cerebral) veins; no lucid interval (i.e., patient did not lose consciousness); crescent-shaped; can be slowly accumulating and heterogenous in appearance due to combination of dried + fresh blood; increased risk in elderly/dementia and alcoholics; answer in acceleration-deceleration injuries (shaken baby syndrome; motor vehicle accidents); NBME wants craniotomy as the answer for Tx (no evidence for mere observation as the answer on any of the USMLE material); if the patient has decreased Glasgow score, do “intubation + hyperventilation” as answer (decreased CO2 → decreased cerebral perfusion → will reduce intracranial pressure) before craniotomy. Epidural (choice B) → rupture of middle meningeal artery (branch of external carotid); lucid interval (i.e., patient lost consciousness then returned to normal → patient goes home thinking he/she is okay and then dies); lens (biconvex) shape; fast accumulating; if low GCS, do “intubation + hyperventilation,” then do craniotomy. If normal GCS, just do craniotomy. Subarachnoid (choice C) → rupture of anterior communicating artery (ACoM) or posterior communicating artery (PCoM) saccular/berry aneurysm; ACoM > PCoM in terms of location; patient often reports “worst headache of his/her life”; PCoM aneurysm classically associated with ipsilateral blown pupil (mydriasis) due to CN III impingement; HTN is most common risk factor in population and accounts for most cases; Ehlers-Danlos and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) are HY non-HTN-associated specific causes of saccular aneurysms. Patient with HTN still more likely to die from myocardial infarction (HTN → atherosclerosis) than saccular aneurysm (asked on NBME). Intracerebral (intraparenchymal) hemorrhage → associated with Alzheimer (amyloid angiopathy especially the answer in Alzheimer patients with recurrent hemorrhagic stroke); also associated with chronic HTN and Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms of lenticulostriate arteries; can be associated with brain cancer as well (e.g., glioblastoma multiforme).

rapidFireQAs.q: 17M + motorcycle accident + severe cognitive impairment two years following accident; based on the following MRI, what is the most likely diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: diffuse axonal injury; caused by shearing forces from rapid-deceleration injury. Note the irregular areas of hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted MRI.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + SLE + the following CT of head shows ring-enhancing lesion; what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: primary CNS lymphoma; the wrong answer is Toxoplasmosis. Ring-enhancing lesions can refer to abscesses, malignancy, Toxo, and neurocysticerosis. Autoimmune diseases (e.g., Hashimoto, SLE, etc.) and immunosuppression (i.e., AIDS) carry increased risk of primary CNS lymphoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + failure to thrive + seizure; based on the following MRI, what’s the most likely diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: pilocytic astrocytoma. Notice the large solid and cystic lesion. The solid component is white (hyperintense) on the MRI; the cystic component is black (hypointense). This is a HY image for Step 1.

rapidFireQAs.q: 54M + 3-month Hx of cognitive disturbance + presents today with seizure; based on the following head CT, what’s the most likely diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: glioblastoma multiforme (butterfly glioma); notice the heterogeneity due to areas of necrosis and hemorrhage; it need not cross the midline, but when it does it is sometimes referred to as “butterfly glioma.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M + developed cataracts at young age + six-month history of left-sided tinnitus and hearing loss; if his diagnosis is the same as that seen in the following gross specimen, what is his most likely underlying genetic condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx is acoustic schwannoma occurring at the cerebellopontine junction; in a young patient, neurofibromatosis type II (NF2) is likely etiology; can progress to be bilateral; if elderly patient, usually sporadic and unilateral.

rapidFireQAs.q: 56M + nine-year Hx of progressive right-sided hearing loss; MRI shows large mass at the cerebellopontine junction; the mass most likely arises from which nerve and cell type?
rapidFireQAs.a: vestibulocochlear nerve and neural crest cells.

rapidFireQAs.q: Looking at the following MRI, what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Chiari malformation, characterized by inferior herniation of the cerebellar tonsils. Note the inferior herniation of the cerebellar tonsils; Chiari type I is characterized by mere herniation and is the answer if the vignette gives you a teenager or young adult; it can also be associated with syringomyelia (syrinx of CSF in the spinal cord). Chiari II (Arnold-Chiari malformation) is more severe and is the answer if the vignette mentions a child who not only has cerebellar herniation but also lumbosacral myelomeningocele of the spinal cord. In other words: Teenager or young adult + syrinx of spinal cord → answer = Chiari I. Child + lumbosacral meningomyelocele → answer = Chiari II (Arnold-Chiari malformation).

rapidFireQAs.q: Learn the following herniation types:
rapidFireQAs.a: HY point is that neural tube defects (spina bifida) occur between 3-4 weeks gestation. The pregnant woman needs adequate folic acid (vitamin B9) prior to and during early pregnancy for prevention. Antiepileptics (i.e., particularly valproic acid, but also phenytoin and carbamazepine) are also associated with neural tube defects. Neural tube defects lead to increased AFP and acetylcholinesterase in CSF.

rapidFireQAs.q: Newborn + myelomeningocele; what is the affected developmental process?
rapidFireQAs.a: “closure of caudal neuropore.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F at 20 weeks gestation + ultrasound shows fetus with anencephaly; what is the mechanism for this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: “failure of closure of rostral neuropore.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate + tuft of hair on midline in lumbar region + palpation of region shows absence of spinous process; what is the mechanism for this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: “failure of fusion of the sclerotomes.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Looking at the following MRI, what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dandy-Walker malformation; all you need to know: this is the answer if the vignette describes absent cerebellar vermis + cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle.

rapidFireQAs.q: Identify the following brain herniation types:
rapidFireQAs.a: A = cingulate (subfalcine) herniation; B = transcalvarial herniation; C = central transtentorial herniation; D = uncal herniation; E = upward transtentorial hernation; F = tonsillar herniation.

rapidFireQAs.q: The area labeled X on the following diagram notably contains a high density of which kind of channel(s) (i.e., Na, Ca, K, etc.)?
rapidFireQAs.a: Area labeled X = node of Ranvier; answer = contains high concentrations of sodium channels.

rapidFireQAs.q: Identify the following cranial nerve lesions:
rapidFireQAs.a: A = lesion of CN III (oculomotor) → presents as down and out; B = CN IV lesion (trochlear) → presents as upward gaze + patient will tilt head toward unaffected side; C = CN VI (abducens) → medially directed eye. PCoM aneurysmal compression of CN III affects superficial parasympathetic efferents leading to ipsilateral mydriasis and loss of accommodation; diabetes may affect deep extraocular muscle efferents leading to partial ptosis and down-and-out pupil.

rapidFireQAs.q: 31F + Hx of multiple sclerosis + presents with the following visual problem; where is the location of her pathology?
rapidFireQAs.a: right parietal lobe (contralateral inferior quadrantanopsia).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + lung cancer + 2-week Hx of progressive loss of vision of the left visual field of both eyes; if MRI of the brain is performed, metastases might be seen where?
rapidFireQAs.a: right occipital Lobe; Dx is homonymous hemianopia.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Can you explain that Marcus-Gunn pupil and optic neuritis stuff?”
rapidFireQAs.a: MG pupil caused by CN II (optic nerve) lesion, classically as a result of optic neuritis in flare of multiple sclerosis; because of the CN II lesion, the intensity of the light is under-sensed by that eye (afferent signal), so the resultant efferent CN III (oculomotor) parasympathetic output (back to the eyes for pupillary constriction) is attenuated; this means when you shine a light in the affected eye, both pupils constrict less in comparison to when the light is shone in the unaffected eye; this gives the mere impression that the pupils dilate when light is shone in the affected eye. Still confusing? Take a look at the following illustration (assuming a lesion of the patient’s right eye [left side of illustration]):

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + presents with the left pupil larger than the right pupil after undergoing cranial surgery; which letter on the following image best reflects the location of his pathology?
rapidFireQAs.a: D (CN III; oculomotor nerve), lesion can cause down and out pupil and/or mydriasis; this illustration of the cavernous sinus is exceedingly HY for Step 1. A = cavernous sinus; B = sphenoid sinus; C = internal carotid artery; E = trochlear nerve (CN IV); F = ophthalmic branch of trigeminal nerve (V1); G = abducens nerve (CN VI); H = maxillary branch of trigeminal nerve (V2).

rapidFireQAs.q: 34M + sinus infection one week ago treated with amoxicillin/clavulanate + now presents with diplopia, ophthalmoplegia, and headache + has fever of 103F; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cavernous sinus thrombosis; sinus infections can ascend to cavernous sinus via the valveless facial veins; the sequence of sinus infection followed by fever, diplopia, and ophthalmoplegia is classic for cavernous sinus thrombosis; give IV antibiotics.

rapidFireQAs.q: 41F + new-onset neurologic dysfunction following surgery of her sphenoid sinus; what additional finding is likely present on the examination?
rapidFireQAs.a: inability to abduct eye (abducens nerve injury); CN VI is most medial / closest to the sphenoid sinus and is susceptible to injury.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + needs to undergo laminectomy; where on the following illustration of a vertebra is the most appropriate location for surgical entrance to the neural canal?
rapidFireQAs.a: E (lamina); A = transverse process; B = pedicle; C = vertebral body; D = facet joints; F = spinous process. Should be noted as a tangential factoid that the vertebral arteries (first branch of subclavians) ascend bilaterally through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae.

rapidFireQAs.q: 17M + undergoing spinal surgery + if needle is inserted posteriorly between L3 and L4 vertebral arches, what ligament must be traversed to reach the spinal canal?
rapidFireQAs.a: Answer = ligamentum Flavum.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + lumbar disc herniation; which spinal ligament is pushed into the spinal root nerves?
rapidFireQAs.a: posterior longitudinal ligament.

rapidFireQAs.q: 63M + pain radiating down distal anterior thigh, knee, medial leg, and medial foot; compression of nerve root in which intervertebral foramina is most likely the cause of her symptoms? → answer = L3-L4.
rapidFireQAs.a: HY dermatomes and reflexes: C5 = biceps jerk; C7 = triceps reflex; T4 = nipples; T10 = umbilicus; L1 = groin; L3/4 = knee jerk; S1 = ankle jerk + sole of foot.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + gestational pemphigoid with itchy vesicles around the umbilicus; her pain is sensed by which dermatome?

52M + sudden loss of vision in right eye + no pain + central scotoma of visual field + fundoscopy shows pale opaque fundus and bright red fovea centralis; 8 months later, if right eye is illuminated, what reaction is most likely to occur in left pupil?
rapidFireQAs.a: “no constriction because retinal ganglion cells in right eye have been destroyed”; normal loop should be CN II of right eye signaling (afferent) to midbrain, with CN III relaying efferent parasympathetic activity back to both eyes to cause both direct and consensual pupillary constriction; in this case, since CN II on the right is disrupted, we would get neither a direct or consensual pupillary constriction in response to light shone in the affected eye; Dx is central retinal artery occlusion leading to cherry red spot on macula; etiology either carotid plaque launching off in setting of HTN or mural thromboembolus secondary to AF; patient experiences permanent painless loss of vision.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + complains of diplopia + can read books normally + decreased adduction in left eye when gazing to the right; what is the likely location of the demyelinating plaque causing these symptoms?
rapidFireQAs.a: left MLF (internuclear ophthalmoplegia).

rapidFireQAs.q: 68M + transient ischemic attack + new-onset anterograde Amnesia; what is the most likely affected location?
rapidFireQAs.a: hippocampus, which is known to be very sensitive to ischemic insult; it is also an answer sometimes for Alzheimer (progressive shrinking of hippocampus and nucleus Basalis of Maynert).

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + left eye pain + blurry vision + progressive weakness of right arm and both legs + fundoscopy shows optic disc swelling + MRI shows multiple T2-weighted bright signal abnormalities in white matter; what cell is attacked by the immune system in this disease?
rapidFireQAs.a: oligodendrocytes; Dx is multiple Sclerosis; mechanism is T cell-mediated destruction of oligodendrocytes in CNS (in contrast, Schwann cell destruction in PNS is Guillain-Barre); oligodendrocytes synthesize myelin in the CNS; Schwann cells synthesize myelin in the PNS (including cranial nerves, which are PNS).
