rapidFireQAs.q: 81M + stroke + which type of cell of CNS is likely to clear necrotic tissue in the affected area?
rapidFireQAs.a: microglial cells (macrophages of the CNS).

rapidFireQAs.q: What cell does HIV infect in the CNS?
rapidFireQAs.a: microglia; microglia in the CNS are one of the major cellular reservoirs of HIV.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + long Hx of alcoholism + stumbles to the right when ambulating + Romberg sign intact; where is the location of his pathology?
rapidFireQAs.a: right side of cerebellum; cerebellar lesions always ipsilateral; lateral aspects of cerebellum result in ipsilateral limb ataxia; midline cerebellar lesions (vermis) result in truncal ataxia; Romberg sign is (+) if etiology for ataxia is dorsal columns (i.e., tabes dorsalis in neurosyphilis); Romberg (-) means cerebellar etiology on USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: 51F + irregular flailing movements of right side of body; Dx and site of lesion?
rapidFireQAs.a: hemiballismus; lesion of contralateral (left) subthalamic nucleus.

rapidFireQAs.q: 7M + ingested substance under the kitchen since + vomiting; what part of the brain is most likely responsible for the vomiting, and where is it located?
rapidFireQAs.a: area postrema, which is a chemotactic trigger zone for emesis; it is located on the dorsal aspect of the medulla at the caudal 4th ventricle.

rapidFireQAs.q: 51M + hereditary hemochromatosis + isolated decrease in serum gonadotropins; where is the most likely location of the pathology?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypothalamus → iron deposition in hypothalamus resulting in decreased GnRH; if deposition were in anterior pituitary, then we’d likely get a decrease in the other anterior pituitary hormones as well, rather than an isolated decrease in LH and FSH.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the hormones secreted by the anterior pituitary?
rapidFireQAs.a: LH, FSH, TSH, ACTH, GH, prolactin.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the hormones stored by the posterior pituitary?
rapidFireQAs.a: vasopressin (ADH), oxytocin; these hormones are not synthesized in the posterior pituitary; they are synthesized in the hypothalamus and then merely stored in the posterior pituitary.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the hormones secreted by the hypothalamus that regulate the anterior pituitary hormones?
rapidFireQAs.a: GnRH (stimulates LH, FSH); TRH (stimulates TSH); CRH (stimulates ACTH); GHRH (stimulates GH); dopamine (inhibits prolactin).

rapidFireQAs.q: 16F + MVA + pituitary stalk is severed; which hormone will increase?
rapidFireQAs.a: prolactin; all hypothalamic hormones are stimulatory except for dopamine’s actions on prolactin, which are inhibitory.

rapidFireQAs.q: 54F + decreased fluency of spontaneous speech after a cerebral infarction + comprehension is normal + examination shows weakness of lower 2/3 of right side of face; Dx? + which vessel did the stroke occur?
rapidFireQAs.a: Broca aphasia; left middle cerebral artery.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + BP 140/100 + 2/5 muscle strength in left leg + brisk reflexes in left leg; which vessel is the most likely site of the stroke?
rapidFireQAs.a: right anterior cerebral artery.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + complains that food has lost its flavor ever since she got hit in the head during a softball game last week; damage to which structure may have occurred?
rapidFireQAs.a: cribriform plate; olfactory nerve lesion leads to decreased perception of taste.

rapidFireQAs.q: 81F + difficulty fastening buttons + weakness of intrinsic muscles of hands + loss of sensation in 5th fingers; Q asks for Dx at level of spine
rapidFireQAs.a: C7-T1 foraminal stenosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + Hx of MS + two-week Hx of severe shooting pain in left cheek brought on by brushing teeth; what is the most likely location of the demyelination leading to this patient’s presentation?
rapidFireQAs.a: pons (giving rise to trigeminal nerve; in this case MS patient with trigeminal neuralgia-like presentation from central lesion).

rapidFireQAs.q: 61F + brought to ER by police after she was wandering around the city confused + disheveled + broad- based gait and nystagmus + results of alcohol and drug screening are negative; brain MRI will show atrophy of what?
rapidFireQAs.a: mammillary bodies; Dx is Wernicke encephalopathy (ACOW → Ataxia, Confusion, Ophthalmoplegia, Wernicke encephalopathy).

rapidFireQAs.q: 55M + two-week Hx of constant and intense pain of left arm + Hx of stroke 5 months ago resulting in loss of sensation to left side of body + examination shows decreased light touch, vibration, pain, and temperature over left side of body; Q asks: cause of this patient’s pain is most likely due to damage to where?
rapidFireQAs.a: right thalamus; thalamic pain syndrome is a HY post-stroke cause of pain.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + struck in left eye by a golf ball + presents with diplopia, periorbital swelling, and enophthalmos + upward gaze is impaired + sensation is decreased over the left zygoma + x-ray shows orbital floor fracture; entrapment of which two muscles best explains this patient’s presentation?
rapidFireQAs.a: inferior rectus and inferior oblique.

rapidFireQAs.q: 77M + sudden-onset miosis of left eye + ptosis of left eyelid + dysphagia + difficulty speaking + pain and Temperature are decreased on left side of her face and right side of body; which artery is most likely occluded?
rapidFireQAs.a: left posterior inferior cerebellar artery; Horner syndrome as associated with PICA infarct (lateral medullary syndrome) is HY.

rapidFireQAs.q: 15M + pain and tingling in her right hand when she goes backpacking + symptoms resolve five minutes after she takes her backpack off; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: thoracic outlet syndrome due to first cervical rib.

rapidFireQAs.q: 26F + tonic-clonic seizure + immediately prior smelled foul odor for several seconds; where did the seizure most likely originate from?
rapidFireQAs.a: temporal lobe.

rapidFireQAs.q: 69M + stroke + hoarse voice + can't detect pinprick or cold on right side of face or left side of body; what’s the location of the stroke?
rapidFireQAs.a: lateral medulla (right PICA); once again, lateral medullary syndrome = PICAchew (Pikachu) → dysphagia/hoarseness +/- Horner syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18M + used “synthetic heroine” at party + tight muscles + shuffling gait + bradykinesia + afebrile and pupils normal; Q asks location of the brain affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: substantia nigra; MPTP-induced Parkinsonism is assessed on both USMLE Step 1; MPTP is sold as “synthetic heroine” and can cause Parkinsonism.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + urinary incontinence + blurry vision + diminished vibration in the toes + unable to maintain balance with eyes closed; Q asks damage to which spinal tract?
rapidFireQAs.a: fasciculus gracilis of the dorsal columns; in contrast, fasciculus cuneatus would do vibration/proprioception of upper limbs; diagnosis here is MS presenting with classic urge incontinence, optic neuritis, and a (+) Romberg sign.

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + moderate strabismus; if not treated, she'll have deficits in depth perception due to lack of appropriate competitive interactions in the visual cortex; calcium entry through which receptor mediates the outcome of this competitive process?
rapidFireQAs.a: Answer = NMDA (glutamate) receptors; yes, weird, but handle it.

rapidFireQAs.q: Newborn + strabismus; what's the rationale for surgically correcting this problem during early childhood?
rapidFireQAs.a: if not, normal binocular vision won't develop.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23M + inferonasal “bleeding” of the pupil + incomplete closure of embryonic fissure of what structure in the right eye is most likely responsible?
rapidFireQAs.a: iris. Student says “?” → CHARGE syndrome presents with coloboma of the eye, where the iris fails to develop properly, resulting in a “bleeding” of the pupil.

rapidFireQAs.q: 57F + invasive gall bladder cancer + 3-week Hx of severe left-sided back and abdominal pain; an operation scheduled to relieve pain would target which spinal tract?
rapidFireQAs.a: right spinothalamic tract (contralateral).

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F + fluoxetine prescribed; benefit occurs due to effects on neurons located where?
rapidFireQAs.a: raphe nuclei (serotonin-secreting neurons).

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + 4-month Hx of abnormal tingling that started in right hand has progressed to right arm and right side of face; cause of her Sx is a lesion located in which cerebral cortex gyri?
rapidFireQAs.a: left post- central (i.e., posterior to the central sulcus, which is where the primary sensory cortex is).

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + progressive ataxia with unsteady gait + left-sided intention tremors; cause is damage to which brain area?
rapidFireQAs.a: left cerebellar hemisphere (cerebellar lesions lead to ipsilateral neurologic signs).

rapidFireQAs.q: 72F + loss of pain and temperature on left side of face and right of the body + paralysis of vocal cords on left + loss of gag reflex on left; what part of the brainstem is most likely affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: left dorsolateral medulla; lateral medullary syndrome; CN IX/V dysfunction; vocal cords are recurrent laryngeal nerves (of vagus); gag reflex is CN IX afferent and CN X efferent.

rapidFireQAs.q: 54F + 4-day Hx of hoarseness and difficulty swallowing + unable to elevate left side of palate; which CN is damaged?
rapidFireQAs.a: left vagus nerve; failure of elevation of ipsilateral palate causes contralateral uvula deviation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 54M + Hx of HTN + unable to recognize people’s face + unable to recognize objects unless he touches them or hears sounds they make; damaged area of brain is supplied by what artery?
rapidFireQAs.a: posterior cerebral artery; prosopagnosia (inability to recognize faces) and visual agnosia (inability to recognize objects upon seeing them) are associated with occipital lobe lesions (PCA infarct).

rapidFireQAs.q: 61F + undergoes repair of leaking saccular aneurysm + postoperative CT scan shows widening of subarachnoid space; what changes in CSF are the most likely cause of these findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased movement of CSF through the arachnoid villi.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + decreased taste to anterior 2/3 of left side of tongue; which nerve is likely damaged?
rapidFireQAs.a: left facial nerve.

rapidFireQAs.q: The thalamus notably does not receive sensory input from which nerve?
rapidFireQAs.a: olfactory nerve.

rapidFireQAs.q: Stroke affecting ventral posterolateral (VPL) & ventral posteromedial (VPM) nuclei of thalamus results in what kind of deficit?
rapidFireQAs.a: pure sensory; VPL senses from body; VPM from face.

rapidFireQAs.q: 59M + Parkinson disease; loss of patient’s substantia nigra is most likely to result in disinhibition in which brain area?
rapidFireQAs.a: striatum.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + uvula deviation to the right + dysphagia; which tongue muscle might be affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: palatoglossus (innervated by CN X); other tongue muscles innervated by CN XII.

rapidFireQAs.q: 29M + MVA + hematoma over mastoid processes bilaterally + rhinorrhea + otorrhea + raccoon eyes; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: base of skull fracture (classic tetrad).

rapidFireQAs.q: 31F + MVA + GCS of 6 + BP 165/90 + RR 10 + HR 55; what is the mechanism for this patient’s hypertension?
rapidFireQAs.a: increased intracranial pressure (Cushing triad of HTN, bradycardia, bradypnea).

rapidFireQAs.q: 59F + metastatic breast cancer + absent corneal reflex on right; metastases to which cranial nerve exit point might be responsible for this neuro exam finding?
rapidFireQAs.a: superior orbital fissure → exit point for ophthalmic branch of trigeminal nerve; V1 → Standing Room Only → Superior orbital fissure, foramen Rotundum, foramen Ovale; for V1, V2, V3, respectively.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + herpes encephalitis + treated with IV acyclovir + months later has hyperphagia, hypersexuality, hyperorality; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Kluver-Bucy syndrome (bilateral amygdala lesions); KB syndrome can be a rare complication of HSV encephalitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 71F + stroke + now has agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right agnosia; what part of the brain did the stroke occur?
rapidFireQAs.a: angular gyrus (parietal lobe); Dx = Gerstmann syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23M + near-drowning episode with hypoxia to brain; what change might be seen in the hippocampi of this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: “red neurons” → pathologic staining pattern of neurons during acute hypoxic injury; hippocampi notably susceptible to ischemia → results in anterograde amnesia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + episodes of feeling like the room is spinning + sometimes associated with vomiting + physician is able to reproduce the Sx with the Dix-Hallpike maneuver; what is the mechanism for this patient’s condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: “posterior semicircular canal otolith”; Dx = benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV); Tx with Epley maneuver.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + viral infection + tinnitus + hearing loss + vertigo; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: labyrinthitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + viral infection + vertigo; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: vestibular neuritis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 31M + warm water instilled into left ear causes nystagmus, but warm water in right ear does not cause nystagmus; where is the site of the lesion? → right-sided vestibular apparatus.
rapidFireQAs.a: Called the vestibular caloric reflex test. Warm water instilled into ear causes endolymph on ipsilateral side to move, mimicking a head turn to the ipsilateral side. This causes eye movement to the contralateral side, with nystagmus back toward the ipsilateral side. Cold water has the opposite effect. This mimics a head turn to the contralateral side, with the eyes moving toward the ipsilateral side, with nystagmus toward the contralateral side. If nystagmus fails to occur with the side that is stimulated (i.e., the side that’s warmer), then there is weakness of the vestibular apparatus on that side.

rapidFireQAs.q: Shining light in either eyes causes direct and consensual pupillary constriction; this clinical maneuver is a test of functional integrity of what?
rapidFireQAs.a: midbrain (Edinger-Westphal nucleus).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + left eye fails to constrict when light is shone in both the left and right eyes; where is the lesion
rapidFireQAs.a: oculomotor nerve (CN III).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + light directed into right eye results in constriction of right pupil but not left pupil + light directed into patient's left eye results in constriction of right pupil but not left pupil; where is the site of the lesion
rapidFireQAs.a: left oculomotor nerve (CN III); same thing as prior Q, but worded differently.

rapidFireQAs.q: 69M + smoker for 50 years + constricted left pupil + left eyelid droopy + skin dry on left side of face; where is the lesion?
rapidFireQAs.a: Pancoast tumor of lung resulting in impingement on superior cervical ganglia (Horner syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + burning vesicular lesions around the lips; Q asks about the mechanism of this pathogen’s presentation
rapidFireQAs.a: NBME answer = “reactivation in sensory neurons” → herpes labialis (HSV1/2) → virus lies dormant in trigeminal nerve (V2 – maxillary branch; V3 – mandibular branch).

rapidFireQAs.q: 3-day-old male + born at home + umbilical cord tied with twine + arching of back; mechanism for disease process?
rapidFireQAs.a: “blockade of inhibitory neurotransmitter release” → tetanus toxin causes decreased presynaptic release of GABA and glycine by inhibiting SNARE protein; USMLE might show you a drawing of where the toxin acts, and the answer is inside the presynaptic terminal. Rinne + Weber tests

rapidFireQAs.q: Diarrhea + Guillain-Barre syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: Campylobacter

rapidFireQAs.q: Guillain-Barré syndrome CSF?
rapidFireQAs.a: albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein + normal cells)

rapidFireQAs.q: Guillain-Barré syndrome Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: electromyography + nerve conduction studies (on NBME)

rapidFireQAs.q: Ataxia, confusion, ophthalmoplegia
rapidFireQAs.a: Wernicke encephalopathy (B1 deficiency)

rapidFireQAs.q: Retrograde amnesia + confabulation in alcoholic
rapidFireQAs.a: Korsakoff psychosis

rapidFireQAs.q: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: mammillary bodies

rapidFireQAs.q: Incontinence in multiple sclerosis patient or perimenopausal
rapidFireQAs.a: urge incontinence

rapidFireQAs.q: Gradual-onset dementia + no sensory or motor dysfunction
rapidFireQAs.a: Alzheimer

rapidFireQAs.q: Mini-mental state exam score low + patient tries to do well
rapidFireQAs.a: Alzheimer Mini-mental state exam score low + patient is apathetic / takes long to perform tasks / does poorly on reverse

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient complains about memory loss
rapidFireQAs.a: normal aging, not Alzheimer

rapidFireQAs.q: First-line Tx for Alzheimer
rapidFireQAs.a: donepezil (cholinesterase inhibitor → increases cholinergic transmission); can also give galantamine or rivastigmine

rapidFireQAs.q: NMDA receptor (glutamate receptor) antagonist used in Alzheimer Tx
rapidFireQAs.a: memantine

rapidFireQAs.q: Visual hallucinations + Parkinsonism + dementia
rapidFireQAs.a: Lewy body dementia

rapidFireQAs.q: Apathy + disinhibition + personality change + dementia
rapidFireQAs.a: frontotemporal dementia (Pick disease)

rapidFireQAs.q: Urinary incontinence + ataxia + CNS dysfunction (wet, wobbly, wacky)
rapidFireQAs.a: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus

rapidFireQAs.q: Wet, wobbly, wacky + Parkinsonism
rapidFireQAs.a: still NPH

rapidFireQAs.q: Parkinsonism in older patient
rapidFireQAs.a: Parkinson disease

rapidFireQAs.q: Parkinsonism + axial dystonia
rapidFireQAs.a: progressive supranuclear palsy

rapidFireQAs.q: Viral infection + tinnitus + vertigo +/- neurosensory hearing loss
rapidFireQAs.a: labrynthitis

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for multiple sclerosis flares
rapidFireQAs.a: IV steroids (IV methylprednisolone)

rapidFireQAs.q: Given to MS patients between flares
rapidFireQAs.a: interferon-beta

rapidFireQAs.q: Incontinence in MS
rapidFireQAs.a: urge (hyperactive detrusor, as mentioned earlier)

rapidFireQAs.q: Hematuria + hemoptysis + “head-itis” (mastoiditis, sinusitis, otitis, nasal septal perforation)
rapidFireQAs.a: Wegener

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of tinea pedis
rapidFireQAs.a: topical terbinafine or topical azole

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of tinea corporis (ring worm)
rapidFireQAs.a: topical azole (clotrimazole or miconazole)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of tinea versicolor
rapidFireQAs.a: topical selenium

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of otitis media
rapidFireQAs.a: Strep pneumo

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of otitis media
rapidFireQAs.a: oral amoxicillin only

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of recurrent OM
rapidFireQAs.a: amoxicillin/clavulanate

rapidFireQAs.q: When to do tympanostomy tube
rapidFireQAs.a: three or more OM in 6 months, or 4 or more in a year

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of otitis externa
rapidFireQAs.a: topical ciprofloxacin + hydrocortisone drops

rapidFireQAs.q: High BP + smoker + TIA or stroke or retinal artery occlusion. How to best decrease stroke risk
rapidFireQAs.a: lisinopril, not smoking cessation

rapidFireQAs.q: Hypertensive pt + stroke
rapidFireQAs.a: do carotid duplex ultrasound

rapidFireQAs.q: Normotensive pt + stroke
rapidFireQAs.a: do ECG; if ECG normal → Holter monitor

rapidFireQAs.q: Prophylaxis for otitis externa (i.e., in someone with continued water exposure, like crew)
rapidFireQAs.a: topical alcohol-acetic acid drops

rapidFireQAs.q: Otitis externa + mastoiditis
rapidFireQAs.a: malignant otitis externa

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of otitis media
rapidFireQAs.a: amoxicillin (amoxicillin/clavulanate [Augmentin] is the wrong answer initially; use Augmentin for recurrent OM)

rapidFireQAs.q: When to do a tympanostomy tube?
rapidFireQAs.a: 3+ OM in a 6-month period or 4+ in a year

rapidFireQAs.q: When do you do CT head before LP in suspected meningitis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Confusion that interferes with neurologic exam / decreased GCS score Seizure Focal neurologic signs (motor or sensory) Papilledema or if the optic fundi cannot be visualized Above reasons indicate potential mass lesion, where if you do an LP you can cause tonsillar herniation and death; if CT negative, proceed cautiously to LP

rapidFireQAs.q: Is tPA ever an answer for anything?
rapidFireQAs.a: Ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours. Must do non-contrast CT of the head to confirm no bleed before giving tPA.

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M has 30 minutes of facial drooping + arm weakness since waking up from a nap
rapidFireQAs.a: amount of time since stroke = amount of time that has passed since he was last known to be normal (i.e., before he went to sleep) → on the USMLE, this situation often means don’t give the tPA.

rapidFireQAs.q: Urge incontinence
rapidFireQAs.a: “hyperactive detrusor,” or “detrusor instability” → needs to run to the bathroom when sticking a key in the front door; needs to run to bathroom when opening car door; answer in multiple sclerosis + menopause (part of vasomotor Sx); can be idiopathic; answer = give oxybutynin (anti-muscarinic) or mirabegron (beta-3 agonist); once again, do not give these drugs in stress incontinence.

rapidFireQAs.q: Woman who works in dental care with vesicle on finger; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: herpetic whitlow → HSV1/2 of the finger → treat with oral acyclovir (in real life will give both oral and topical; on the USMLE, answer is always oral)

rapidFireQAs.q: 14M + ataxia + cognitive decline over a few months
rapidFireQAs.a: glue, not alcohol → no way a kid that young would get alcoholic cerebellar ataxia; this is on the NBME even if you find it stupid/weird.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for spasticity in MS
rapidFireQAs.a: baclofen.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of MS
rapidFireQAs.a: choose MRI over CSF IgG oligoclonal bands if both are listed.

rapidFireQAs.q: Urinary incontinence in MS
rapidFireQAs.a: urge incontinence (hyperactive detrusor / detrusor instability)

rapidFireQAs.q: AV-nicking on fundoscopy
rapidFireQAs.a: hypertensive retinopathy

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + drooping of left side of face + decreased muscle strength and increased tendon reflexes of both left upper and lower extremities + Babinski on left + intact sensation; what’s the most likely explanation for this patient’s condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: lacunar infarct of internal capsule; produces “pure motor” stroke in most cases of posterior capsule infarct; thalamic stroke produces “pure sensory” effects; lacunar infarcts are usually due to Hx of HTN causes lipohyalinosis of lenticulostriate arteries.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F undergoing chemotherapy + has low leukocyte count; what drug will help this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: pegfilgrastim (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor; G-CSF); will cause an increase in neutrophils.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + 3-day Hx of paresthesias of the legs + difficulty swallowing + diminished tendon reflexes + CSF shows protein of 70 mg/dL and cell count of 5/uL; what’s the mechanism for this patient’s condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: “destruction of myelin and endoneurial lymphocytic infiltrates”; USMLE wants you to know this description of Guillain-Barre; CSF findings are albuminocytologic dissociation (increased protein but normal cells).

rapidFireQAs.q: 39M + bilateral renal enlargement + high blood pressure + father died from subarachnoid hemorrhage; this patient most likely has a gene mutation in which protein?
rapidFireQAs.a: polycystin; diagnosis is ADPKD; high blood pressure is from cysts impinging on the renal microvasculature leading to surges in RAAS.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + subarachnoid hemorrhage; Q asks biggest risk factor
rapidFireQAs.a: HTN most common overall in general population; otherwise, if patient has ADPKS or Ehlers-Danlos, those would be more specific.

rapidFireQAs.q: 82F + wobbly gait for 4 months + head CT shows crescent-shaped bleed; what is biggest risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: diagnosis is subdural hematoma; often slow-accumulating; elderly have reduced cerebral volume, making superior cerebral (bridging) veins more susceptible to friability; other notable risk factors are alcoholism, dementia (further reduction in brain mass), deceleration injury (car accident or shaken- baby syndrome). There is no lucid interval.

rapidFireQAs.q: 81M + Alzheimer + recurrent hemorrhagic stroke; what is major risk factor for the bleeds?
rapidFireQAs.a: Alzheimer → can lead to amyloid angiopathy, causing intracerebral/intraparenchymal hemorrhage that presents as recurrent hemorrhagic stroke.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + uses a variety of illicit drugs + develops Parkinsonism; risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: MPTP use (synthetic heroin) can cause Parkinsonism.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + eating clay, starch, and ice; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: pica due to iron deficiency.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + ataxia + confusion + ophthalmoplegia + confabulations; what is risk factor for this condition
rapidFireQAs.a: alcoholism causing thiamine deficiency, resulting in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (WKS). ACOW → Ataxia, Confusion, Ophthalmoplegia = Wernicke. If we add confabulations (Korsakoff psychosis) on top of ACOW, we now call it WKS.

rapidFireQAs.q: 60F + lung cancer + difficulty getting up from chair a few times; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: Lambert-Eaton due to small cell (anti-presynaptic voltage-gated Ca channel antibodies).

rapidFireQAs.q: 60F + lung cancer + ataxia; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: small cell cerebellar dysfunction (anti-Hu/-Yo) Abs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + worsening diplopia, dysphagia, and eyelid ptosis over the course of a day; Dx and risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: myasthenia gravis (Abs against post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors); often idiopathic, but can be due to thymoma as risk factor.
